title: Minimum Cost to Equalize Array
statement:
You get an integer array `nums` and two prices, `cost1` and `cost2`. Any number of times, in any order, you may either raise one element of `nums` by 1 and pay `cost1`, or raise two elements at different indices by 1 each and pay `cost2`. Values can never go down.

Find the cheapest total price that makes every element of `nums` equal. That minimum can be huge, so return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.
signature: int minCostToEqualizeArray(int[] nums, int cost1, int cost2)
notes:
## Intuition

Fix the final value `target` (at least the maximum). Element `i` needs `target - nums[i]` raises; let `total` be their sum and `largest = target - low` the biggest need. When `cost2 < 2 · cost1` we want as many pairs as possible. If no need exceeds half of `total`, every raise can be paired except one when `total` is odd. Otherwise the biggest need dominates: each other raise pairs with it and the rest of it is done singly. A higher target gives the others more raises to pair with the dominant one, so it can be cheaper, but past `2 · max` it never helps, so we try every target in between.

## Approach

1. Find `high`, `low` and `sum` in one pass.
2. With at most two elements a pair raise never closes their gap, and with `2 · cost1 <= cost2` pairs never save money: raise everything to `high` singly, paying `(n · high - sum) · cost1`.
3. Otherwise, for each `target` from `high` to `2 · high`, compute `total = n · target - sum` and `largest = target - low`.
4. If `2 · largest <= total`, pay `floor(total / 2)` pairs and `total % 2` singles; otherwise `pairs = total - largest` pairs and `largest - pairs` singles.
5. Keep the minimum in `best` and return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [4, 1]`, `cost1 = 5`, `cost2 = 2`. The pass gives `high = 4`, `low = 1`, `sum = 5`. Since `n = 2`, step 2 applies: `n · high - sum = 3` raises, all on the `1`, at 5 each: `15`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + max(nums)): one pass over `nums`, then O(1) work per target.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Stopping at `target = max` is wrong: for `[1, 5, 5]` with `cost1 = 10`, `cost2 = 1`, target 5 costs 40 but target 9 costs only 8.
- Take the minimum of the true costs first and the modulo last; reduced costs compare wrongly.
- At LeetCode's full size a cost can reach about 10^17: use 64-bit integers in Java and C, and BigInt in JavaScript. Here arrays hold at most 2,000 values, so plain numbers stay exact.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD`, `n` | the modulus 10^9 + 7 and the length of `nums` |
| `high`, `low`, `sum` | maximum, minimum and sum of `nums` |
| `target` | the final common value being tried |
| `total` | raises needed in all to reach `target` |
| `largest` | raises needed by the smallest element |
| `pairs` | pair raises when the smallest element dominates |
| `cost`, `best` | price for this target, and the cheapest so far |
